newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian CPI falls again in May, reaches 1.6 percent.
newsitem.headline: Italian CPI falls again in May, reaches 1.6 percent.

text.p: Italian inflation fell to 1.6 percent in May, its lowest level since February 1969 when it was 1.4 percent, national statistics office Istat said on Wednesday.
The figure was at the high end of market expectations after preliminary data from 11 sample cities had pointed to a consumer price index of 1.5 or 1.6 percent year-on-year for May.
Year-on-year inflation was 1.7 percent in April and 4.3 percent in May 1996. May CPI rose 0.3 percent month-on-month.

The data followed a warning from Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio last Saturday that although inflationary expectations had been beaten, "the flames of inflation have not been completely extinguished".

Fazio, who has resisted lowering interest rates despite steady falls in inflation, told the bank's annual assembly that he was aiming to keep inflation below two percent in 1998. The official discount rate is currently at 6.75 percent.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government last Friday unveiled an ambitious CPI target of 1.8 percent for next year in its latest three-year economic plan.
Fazio said he would not hesitate to tighten monetary policy at the first hint of a reawaking of inflation.
"In the presence of unfavourable developments we will not hesitate to halt our policy of reflation, in extreme cases to change its course," he said.
